Ajantā
------------------------------------------
Celebrated for its cave-paintings, अजन्ता is actually a range of hills in the Ahmednagar district of Maharashtra State. It was originally known as Ājīntha.
अजन्ता">Caves at AjantāThe caves are situated at a distance of 6.5 kms. (4 miles) from the village Fardapur, which itself is 101 kms. (63 miles) from Aurangabad, the district head-quarters.
They are excavated in the semicircular scarp of a steep rock, about 76 metres (250 ft.) high overlooking a narrow sinuous gorge, through which flows a stream called Waghora, descending at the head of a ravine as a waterfall.
अजन्ता">Waterfalls at AjantāThere are 30 caves in all including the unfinished ones. They must have been carved out during the period, 2nd century B. C. to the 7th century A. D.
Some of them contain inscriptions which are also dated.
The caves were probably excavated for the use of the Buddhist (Hīnayāna) मोन्क्स् for their retreat in the rainy season.
Some of them are caityas (See CAITYA.) whereas the others are vihāras (monasteries).
A remarkable feature of these caves is the paintings on their frescoes. They depict the various episodes of बुद्ध’s life as also a few aspects of the contempo-rary social life. The 16th, 17th and the 19th caves contain some remarkable paintings.
The caves contain charming sculptural decorations also.

ajapā-japa
(‘silent repetition’)
------------------------------------------
Japa (repetition of the name of God) is considered to be one of the easiest and most efficacious means of attaining spiritual illumination. Lord कृष्ण goes to the extent of identifying himself with it and calls it a यज्ञ or sacrifice (Bhagavadgītā 10.25). When जप is practised constantly and continuously, practically with every breath, it gets merged as it were with the process of breathing itself. Such an unconscious and automatic जप is christened ‘ajapā-जप.’
Though theoretically, any मन्त्र pertaining to any deity can be chosen for this purpose, in practice this is always confined to the ‘haṁsamantra.’ ‘Haṁsaḥ’ is the abbreviation of ‘ahaṁ saḥ’ (‘I am He’) or its more well-known form “so’ham” (‘He, I am’). With every inhalation the syllable ‘haṁ’ is repeated and with every exhalation the syllable saḥ. Deliberate and conscious practice of this will gradually result in automatic and unconscious repetition coeval with breathing. It is only then that it becomes ‘ajapājapa.’
“Haṁ-saḥ” or “so’ham” is actually the same as the महावाक्यस् (the great dicta of the Upaniṣads—See MAHĀVĀKYAS for details.) aham brahma asmi (‘I am ब्रह्मन्’) or tat tvam asi (‘You are That’). In these statements ‘aham’ or ‘tvam’ represents the जीव or the individual सोउल्; ‘brahma’ or ‘tat’ stand for the Supreme सोउल् or the Absolute. Since the two are apparently poles apart, they can never be identical. However, when only their essential characteristic, viz., चैतन्य or pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is considered, they can be considered identical or as the same.
According to the तन्त्रस्, ‘ham’ repre-sents the शिव principle and ‘saḥ’ represents the शक्ति principle. So ‘haṁsaḥ’ stands for their union and the entire universe created from that union.
Literally हṁस means a swan. Swan is the vehicle of ब्रह्मा the creator. Haṁ and saḥ represent the inspired and expired breath. Everything movable and immovable “breathes” or vibrates and hence can be denoted by ‘haṁsa.’ Therefore it is meet that ब्रह्मा the creative aspect of the Supreme Self is represented as seated thereon.
The Haṁsopaniṣad (15) describes the cosmic form of God using the हṁस imagery to facilitate meditation. The same Upaniṣad also relates the experiences that arise as a result of the ajapājapa of हṁस-मन्त्र (16).
Repetition of the हṁस-मन्त्र or ajapājapa is also known as Ajapāhaṁsa-vidyā.

ajaḍa
(‘that which is not inert’)
------------------------------------------
Literally the word अजड stands for any active and sentient principle as opposed to jaḍa, the inactive and the insentient. However it is used as a technical term in the Viśiṣṭādvaita school of philosophy, the chief exponent of which was Rāmānuja (A.

-1137). द्रव्य or substance can be divided into two groups: jaḍa and अजड. प्रकृति or nature and kāla, or time are grouped under jaḍa. ईश्वर (God), जीव (individual सोउल्), nityavibhūti (immaterial infinite domain of ईश्वर) and धर्मभूतज्ञान (attributive चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of the jīvas) are classed under अजड.
See also VIŚIṢṬĀDVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA.

Ajagava
------------------------------------------
It is the mighty bow of Lord शिव better known as पिनाक.
See PINĀKA for details.

Ajāmila
------------------------------------------
Every saint has a past and every sinner a future. Tears of repentance wash off the sins. Lord’s name purifies even the vilest of sinners. A typical example of transformation is अजामिल whose legend inspires the devotees of God even today.
Bhāgavata, the classic scripture of devotion and spiritual wisdom, recounts the ancient tale of अजामिल (6.1 and 2) and glorifies devotion to विष्णु.
Born and brought up as a pious ब्राह्मण, he once fell a victim to the infatuations of a slave girl and married her after deserting his legally wedded wife and children born of that wedlock. To maintain her and the brood of her children, he took to sinful ways of life like cheating and robbery. When he lay in his deathbed he saw the fierce-looking messengers of यम (the king of death), got frightened and started calling his last son, नारायण by name. The very utterance of this name, being the name of Lord विष्णु, brought His servants also on the scene. Then as विष्णु’s servants intervened on behalf of अजामिल (since what he had uttered was the divine name, the very utterance of which destroys all sins) there ensued a dialogue between them and the messengers of यम. Hearing this dialogue wherein the glory of the divine name was extolled, अजामिल broke down with repentance. Strangely enough he recovered, but repaired to the bank of the sacred river गङ्गा, practised severe austerities, engaged himself in the repetition of the divine name and attained लिबेरतिओन् after death.

ajātivāda
(‘doctrine of non-origination’)
------------------------------------------
Creation of the world is one of the fundamental problems invariably discussed in the Indian philosophical systems. In whichever way a system posits the basic reality—as one or many—from which the world has evolved, logical and ontological difficulties can never be avoided. गौडपाद (7th cent. A. D.) the गुरु of शङ्कर’s preceptor, and the famous author of the Kārikās (concise commentary in verses) on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad has successfully tackled this problem by denying the problem itself!
Considered as the earliest writer on Advaita Vedānta, गौडपाद takes the extreme view that ब्रह्मन् or आत्मन् alone is the only reality that exists and hence neither the world nor the जीव (individual self) ever comes into being. Since ब्रह्मन् has no birth (jāti = birth or origination) nor modification, his doctrine is termed ajātivāda (Kārikās 4.71).
Brahman alone is real. Anyone who sees the world of duality as existing and tries to discover its origination from ब्रह्मन् is trying to ‘see the footprints of the birds in the sky’ (ibid 4.28)!
Gauḍapāda establishes his ajātivāda basing his arguments on the śrutis (revealed scriptures viz., the उपनिषद्स्) as well as लोगिच् and reasoning. He admits that the उपनिषद्स् have described च्रेअतिओन् but avers that they have never declared it to be real (3.15). The main purport of such statements is to emphasize the non-dual Reality behind this apparent diversity.
After successfully countering the arguments of all other schools and establishing his ajātivāda, गौडपाद goes to the extent of denying even ajāti! Since the very concept of an external world which includes the so-called revealed scriptures, is an इल्लुसिओन्, even the theory of ajāti established on the basis of such scriptures and लोगिच्, is an इल्लुसिओन्! From the highest standpoint, the आत्मन् is not aja (unborn) also. He is beyond all relative descriptions and hence defies all such attempts (4.74).
See also GAUḌAPĀDA and MĀṆḌŪKYA-KĀRIKĀ.

Ajātaśatru
(‘One whose enemy is not born’)
------------------------------------------
A term often met with in Sanskrit works, it means ‘one whose enemy is not born.’ It can refer to anyone who is so great and mighty that cannot be challenged by any as an enemy. More often it signifies a man who is so good, compassionate and noble that none hates him. युधिष्ठिर, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas possessed such qualities and hence is known by that name.
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad mentions one अजातशत्रु, the king of काशी (2.1) who was a great jñāni and who taught the ṛṣi Dṛpta बालाकि. The story is repeated in the Kauṣītaki ब्राह्मण Upaniṣad (4.1) also.
According to the Buddhist lore, अजातशत्रु, the son of king Bimbisāra, and a ruler of Magadha committed several heinous crimes, repented of them and approached the बुद्ध for solace. It was on this occasion that the बुद्ध taught the well-known Sāmāññaphala Sutta.
The fortress of Pāṭalīputra, the capital of Magadha, was built by him.

aja
(‘unborn,’ ‘uncreated’)
------------------------------------------
Etymologically the word means that which is unborn or uncreated. Hence it is applied to all the three deities of the Hindu Trinity viz., ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and शिव. It is also applied to the आत्मन् or the self since according to the Hindu scriptures, it is uncreated.
In the Vedic liturgical works, the word denotes the he-goat, considered sacred to पूषन् (an aspect of Sun) and associated with the sacrificial horse in the अश्वमेध (horse-sacrifice) which is believed to lead the horse to the next world. The skin of a sacrificed goat was used in the Vedic funerary rites for laying the dead body.
In अस्त्रोनोम्य् ‘aja’ indicates the sign Aries.
The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (4.5) compares प्रकृति or nature to ajā (she-goat) of three hues (red, white and black, an obvious reference to the three guṇas of सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्) and the jīvātman to aja (he-goat) and depicts him as the enjoyer of प्रकृति.
